highlights: Linear Array Allocation: Sequential memory addressing with $O(1)$ direct access via formula $\text{Loc}(A[i]) = B + i \times W$, where $B$ is base address and $W$ is element word size.
Array Operation Constraints: Fixed static sizing in C/C++; element insertion or deletion at arbitrary index requires $O(n)$ data shifting to maintain contiguity.
Singly Linked List Mechanics: Dynamic nodes holding data and forward pointer $next$; insertions at head take $O(1)$ time, while random access requires $O(n)$ traversal.
Doubly Linked List Traversal: Contains $prev$ and $next$ pointers enabling bidirectional navigation; requires $2 \times$ pointer memory overhead per node.
Circular Linked List Architecture: Tail node links directly to head node ($tail\to next = head$); ideal for round-robin CPU scheduling and circular buffers.
Skip Lists: Probabilistic multi-level forward linked structures achieving $O(\log n)$ average search, insertion, and deletion times.
Memory Locality vs Pointer Overhead: Contiguous arrays optimize CPU cache line spatial locality, whereas linked lists induce pointer indirection and cache misses.
Memory Management & Leaks: Unreferenced heap nodes must be explicitly deallocated using `free()` or `delete` to prevent progressive memory leaks.
Sparse Matrix Storage: Compresses $m \times n$ matrices with predominantly zero entries into 3-tuple coordinate format $(row, col, value)$ or orthogonal linked lists.
University Exam Blueprint: Draw clean box-and-pointer diagrams showing node boundaries, pointer arrows, and terminal NULL ground symbols.
keyPoints: 1D Address Calculation: $\text{Loc}(A[i]) = \text{Base} + i \times W$; Row-major 2D: $\text{Base} + (i \cdot C + j) \cdot W$.
Insertion at Head: Create node, set $node\to next = head$, update $head = node$; Time complexity $O(1)$.
Doubly Linked Deletion: $curr\to prev\to next = curr\to next$ and $curr\to next\to prev = curr\to prev$; Time $O(1)$.
Floyd Cycle Detection: Slow pointer advances 1 step, fast pointer advances 2 steps; collision detects loop in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.
Array vs List Trade-Off: Arrays provide $O(1)$ index access but $O(n)$ insert/delete; Linked lists provide $O(1)$ insert/delete at pointer but $O(n)$ access.
Sentinel Head Node: A dummy head node eliminates edge-case conditional branching during list insertions and deletions.
Polynomial Addition: Traverse two sorted linked lists by exponents, summing coefficients in $O(n + m)$ linear time.
Amortized Array Resizing: Geometric doubling from capacity $C$ to $2C$ guarantees $O(1)$ amortized insertion cost.
Common Bug: Segmentation fault caused by dereferencing NULL pointers ($curr\to next$ when $curr == NULL$).
Exam Tip: In linked list algorithm questions, always state boundary checks for empty lists ($head == NULL$) and single-node lists.

highlights: Stack LIFO Protocol: Last-In First-Out abstract data type supporting $O(1)$ operations: $push(x)$, $pop()$, and $peek()$ executed exclusively at $top$.
Array vs Linked Stack: Array implementation uses fixed size with top index (overflow when $top == MAX - 1$); linked stack dynamically prepends nodes at head.
Arithmetic Expression Notations: Infix ($A + B$), Prefix ($+ A B$), and Postfix ($A B +$ Reverse Polish Notation); removes syntactic ambiguity without parentheses.
Shunting-Yard Algorithm: Dijkstra's parsing algorithm converts infix expressions into postfix notation using an operator precedence stack in $O(n)$ time.
Call Stack & Recursion Management: Activation record frames store parameters, local variables, and return addresses; excessive recursion depth triggers stack overflow.
Queue FIFO Protocol: First-In First-Out abstract data type supporting $enqueue(x)$ at $rear$ and $dequeue()$ at $front$ in $O(1)$ time.
Circular Queue Dynamics: Resolves false overflow in linear array queues by wrapping indices using modulo arithmetic: $rear = (rear + 1) \bmod N$.
Double-Ended Queue (Deque): Allows insertion and deletion at both ends; foundational structure for sliding window maximum and work-stealing schedulers.
Priority Queue Implementations: Elements dequeued by priority rank; implemented via binary min/max heaps with $O(\log n)$ insert and extract.
Industrial Engineering Applications: Stacks power undo/redo buffers and browser history; queues govern network packet buffers and printer spoolers.
keyPoints: Stack Overflow & Underflow: Overflow when $top == MAX - 1$; Underflow when $top == -1$.
Postfix Evaluation: Scan left-to-right; push operands; when operator arrives, pop 2 operands, evaluate $b \text{ op } a$, and push result.
Parentheses Matching: Push opening brackets; on closing bracket, match top of stack and pop; string is balanced if stack is empty at end.
Circular Queue Full Condition: $(rear + 1) \bmod N == front$; Empty condition: $front == -1$.
Queue via Two Stacks: Enqueue pushes to Stack 1; Dequeue pops from Stack 2 (refilling from Stack 1 when empty); Amortized time $O(1)$.
Monotonic Stack: Computes Next Greater Element (NGE) for all elements in an array in $O(n)$ linear time.
Breadth-First Search (BFS): Graph exploration relies fundamentally on a FIFO queue to discover equidistant frontier vertices.
Heap Priority Queue Complexity: Insert $O(\log n)$, Extract-Min $O(\log n)$, Find-Min $O(1)$.
Recursion Unrolling: Any recursive algorithm can be converted into an iterative version by manually managing an auxiliary stack.
Exam Trace Table: For expression conversion, always construct a trace table with columns: Symbol, Stack Contents, and Postfix Output.

highlights: Binary Tree Architecture: Non-linear hierarchical structure where each parent node has at most two children ($left$ and $right$); height $h$ has at most $2^{h+1}-1$ nodes.
Binary Search Tree (BST) Invariant: For every node $u$, all keys in $left(u) < key(u) < right(u)$; average search time is $O(\log n)$, degrading to $O(n)$ when skewed.
AVL Tree Height Balancing: Enforces balance factor $BF = h_L - h_R \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$; restores balance via LL, RR, LR, RL rotations in $O(\log n)$ time.
Red-Black Tree Properties: Self-balancing BST with node colors (root is black, red nodes have black children, identical black-height); guarantees height $h \le 2\log_2(n+1)$.
Tree Traversal Orders: Inorder ($L-Root-R$ outputs sorted BST keys), Preorder ($Root-L-R$), Postorder ($L-R-Root$), and Level-order (BFS queue-driven).
Graph Data Structures: Adjacency Matrix uses $O(V^2)$ memory with $O(1)$ edge checks; Adjacency List uses $O(V + E)$ memory, optimal for sparse topologies.
Graph Traversal Algorithms: Depth-First Search (DFS) uses recursion/stack with discovery/finish timestamps; Breadth-First Search (BFS) finds unweighted shortest paths.
Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): Spans all vertices with minimum total edge weight without cycles; Kruskal's uses Disjoint Set Union ($O(E \log E)$), Prim's uses priority queue ($O(E \log V)$).
Single-Source Shortest Path: Dijkstra's greedy algorithm solves non-negative weighted graphs in $O((V+E)\log V)$; Bellman-Ford accommodates negative weights in $O(V \cdot E)$.
Topological Sorting & DAGs: Linear ordering of vertices in Directed Acyclic Graphs such that edge $(u, v)$ implies $u$ precedes $v$; solved via Kahn's BFS or DFS finish times.
keyPoints: AVL Tree Height Bound: Maximum height $h < 1.44 \log_2(n + 2)$; strictly balanced compared to Red-Black trees.
AVL Rotations: Single rotation for LL and RR; Double rotation for LR (left-rotate child, right-rotate parent) and RL.
BST Inorder Invariant: Inorder traversal of a valid Binary Search Tree strictly produces ascending sorted output.
Complete vs Full Binary Tree: Full tree: every node has 0 or 2 children; Complete tree: all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left-to-right.
Dijkstra's Limitation: Fails on graphs containing negative edge weights; requires non-negative edge weights $w(u, v) \ge 0$.
Bellman-Ford Cycle Detection: Relaxes all edges $V-1$ times; a successful relaxation on the $V$-th pass confirms a negative-weight cycle.
Kruskal's MST Greedy Step: Sort edges by weight; insert edge if endpoints belong to different disjoint sets using `find` and `union`.
Eulerian Path Condition: Connected undirected graph has an Euler path iff exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degrees.
Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs: Dynamic programming recurrence: $D^{(k)}[i][j] = \min(D^{(k-1)}[i][j], D^{(k-1)}[i][k] + D^{(k-1)}[k][j])$.
Exam Tip: When drawing AVL tree insertions, write the balance factor beside every ancestor node before performing rotations.

highlights: Sequential vs Binary Search: Linear search operates in $O(n)$ time on unsorted data; Binary search halves the search space each step, requiring $O(\log n)$ on sorted arrays.
Quadratic Comparison Sorts: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort run in $O(n^2)$ worst-case; Insertion Sort runs in $O(n)$ linear time on nearly sorted inputs.
Merge Sort Divide-and-Conquer: Divides array into halves, recursively sorts, and merges in $O(n)$ time; guaranteed $O(n \log n)$ time with $O(n)$ auxiliary memory.
Quick Sort Partitioning: Selects a pivot element, partitions into lower/higher segments; average runtime is $O(n \log n)$, degrading to $O(n^2)$ when pivot selection is extremal.
Heap Sort Mechanism: Builds a binary max-heap in $O(n)$ time, repeatedly swaps root with last element and heapifies in $O(\log n)$; in-place and non-stable $O(n \log n)$.
Comparison Sort Lower Bound: Any deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm requires at least $\Omega(n \log n)$ comparisons in the worst case via decision tree theorem.
Linear Time Non-Comparison Sorts: Counting Sort ($O(n + k)$), Radix Sort ($O(d(n + k))$), and Bucket Sort exploit key digit structures to beat the comparison lower bound.
Sorting Stability: A sorting algorithm is stable if elements with duplicate keys preserve their original relative input order (e.g. Merge Sort, Insertion Sort).
External Sorting Multi-Way Merge: Used when data exceeds RAM capacity; files are split into sorted runs in memory and merged using loser trees.
Industrial Implementations: Hybrid sorting engines like Timsort (Python / Java) combine Insertion Sort and Merge Sort to optimize real-world performance.
keyPoints: Binary Search Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) \implies T(n) = O(\log n)$; mid computed as $low + (high - low)/2$ to prevent integer overflow.
Quick Sort Recurrence: Average case $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) \implies O(n \log n)$; Worst case $T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) \implies O(n^2)$.
Merge Sort Space Complexity: Requires $O(n)$ extra buffer space for arrays; linked lists can be merge sorted in $O(1)$ auxiliary memory.
Heapify Time Complexity: Sifting down takes $O(h)$; building heap from raw array takes $\sum \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} O(h) = O(n)$ linear time.
Stability Classification: Stable: Insertion Sort, Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Counting Sort; Unstable: Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Selection Sort.
Hoare vs Lomuto Partitioning: Hoare's scheme uses two converging pointers, performing $3\times$ fewer swaps on average than Lomuto's single pointer.
Dutch National Flag: Edsger Dijkstra's 3-way partitioning sorts arrays of 0s, 1s, and 2s in a single pass with $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.
Radix Sort Stability Requirement: The underlying sub-routine sorting individual digits must be strictly stable (typically Counting Sort).
In-Place Definition: An algorithm is in-place if it requires $O(1)$ or at most $O(\log n)$ auxiliary recursion stack space beyond input storage.
Big-O Summary Table: Memorize Best, Average, Worst Time, and Auxiliary Space for all 7 major sorting algorithms for written exams.

highlights: Hash Function Mapping: Maps arbitrary large keys from universe $U$ into table slots $0 \le h(k) < m$; must be deterministic, uniform, and fast ($O(1)$).
Division & Multiplication Hash Methods: Division method $h(k) = k \bmod m$ (with $m$ prime); Multiplication method $h(k) = \lfloor m (k A \bmod 1) \rfloor$ with Knuth's constant $A \approx 0.618033$.
Separate Chaining Collision Resolution: Each table slot references a linked list of colliding entries; average lookup time is $O(1 + \alpha)$ where load factor $\alpha = n/m$.
Open Addressing Probing Techniques: All keys reside directly in table slots; Linear Probing ($h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) \bmod m$) suffers from primary clustering.
Quadratic Probing & Double Hashing: Quadratic probing resolves primary clustering; Double hashing uses two independent hash functions ($h(k, i) = (h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \bmod m$).
Asymptotic Complexity Notations: Big-O ($O$, asymptotic upper bound), Big-Omega ($\Omega$, lower bound), Big-Theta ($\Theta$, tight bound), Little-o ($o$), and Little-omega ($\omega$).
Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer: Solves recurrences $T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)$ by comparing driving function $f(n)$ against critical polynomial $n^{\log_b a}$.
Amortized Complexity Techniques: Analyzes average cost per operation over worst-case sequence; methods include Aggregate method, Accounting method, and Potential function method.
Bloom Filters & Probabilistic Hashing: Space-efficient probabilistic bit-array testing set membership; guarantees zero false negatives with controllable false positive rate.
Industrial Hash Architectures: Distributed consistent hashing in Amazon DynamoDB and Apache Cassandra minimizes key remapping during cluster node resizing.
keyPoints: Load Factor Formula: $\alpha = \frac{n}{m}$; for separate chaining $\alpha$ can exceed 1; for open addressing $\alpha < 1$ must be strictly maintained.
Double Hashing Coprimality: $h_2(k)$ must be relatively prime to table size $m$ (typically $m$ is chosen as a prime number) to probe all slots.
Master Theorem Case 1: If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$ for $\epsilon > 0$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$.
Master Theorem Case 2: If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$ for $k \ge 0$, then $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)$.
Master Theorem Case 3: If $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ and satisfies regularity condition $a f(n/b) \le c f(n)$ for $c < 1$, then $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$.
Table Dynamic Resizing: When load factor $\alpha$ crosses threshold (e.g. 0.75), allocate a table of double prime size and re-hash all existing keys.
Bloom Filter Guarantee: Never produces false negatives (if filter returns false, item is definitely absent from the set).
Universal Hashing: Randomly selecting a hash function from a universal family guarantees expected collision count between distinct keys is $\le 1/m$.
Amortized Dynamic Array: Inserting $n$ elements into an array with geometric doubling takes $O(n)$ total work, yielding $O(1)$ amortized insert cost.
Exam Notation Checklist: When writing asymptotic proofs, always state the positive constants $c_1, c_2, n_0$ and the corresponding inequality.
